name: Satin Sheen Gold
lede: Satin Sheen Gold is a muted, brownish gold from the extended web color lists, its name describing a fabric finish rather than any coiner or standard on record.

sections.title: A finish word, not a pedigree
sections.body:
Our library carries Satin Sheen Gold only as a Wikipedia-sourced crowd-list entry, with no dictionary, dye house or company credited and no first-recorded date [1]. "Satin" and "sheen" both describe surface finish, a soft, low-glare gloss, rather than naming a pigment, mineral or place, so the color is filed here as a descriptive compound built on the base word "gold" [1]. Several low-quality color-reference sites online repeat an unsourced claim tying the name to a television costume; it is not corroborated by any institutional source and is left out here [2].

By our look-alike data the nearest color is [[mustard|Mustard]], 2.6 units away and read as more vivid, with [[goldenrod|Goldenrod]] further off at 3.6, also more vivid [3]. Against the library's own curriculum colors it sits closest to Mustard as well [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to this gold in 423 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.8 percent, as photographed [4]. The strongest single match is Maurice Denis's 1890 *Le Christ vert*, where it covers 68 percent of the canvas, and the earliest is a 1230 crucifix panel, at 6 percent [4]. The 1820s decade carries a real lift, 46 hits across 731 paintings from that decade, well above the archive's overall rate [4]. George Dawe, Paul Sérusier and Pierre Bonnard are the painters most disproportionately associated with it, and India is the most disproportionate country, with 63 hits across 721 paintings [4]. All of this is a computed color match on varnished, photographed canvases, not a pigment identification [4].
